test.topicName: Core Web Vitals: LCP, CLS, INP — definitions, thresholds, improvements

questions.question: Which of the following can be considered the Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) element on a page?
options: A) An element, the poster image of a
B) Any DOM node, including <script> and <meta> tags
C) Only elements — no other element type is eligible
D) Only elements that are above the fold at any viewport size, regardless of type
questions.correctAnswer: A) An element, the poster image of a
questions.explanation: The LCP algorithm considers a specific set of element types as candidates: , inside

questions.question: What aspect of user experience does Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) measure?
options: A) Unexpected visual instability — how much visible content shifts position during the page's lifecycle without user-initiated interaction
B) The total time until the page becomes interactive
C) The delay between a user's input and the browser's response
D) The number of DOM nodes repainted per second
questions.correctAnswer: A) Unexpected visual instability — how much visible content shifts position during the page's lifecycle without user-initiated interaction
questions.explanation: CLS sums the layout shift scores (impact fraction × distance fraction) of every unexpected layout shift that occurs during the page's lifespan, excluding shifts that happen within 500ms of a user interaction (which are considered expected). It quantifies visual stability, not load speed or responsiveness.

questions.question: In March 2024, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) officially replaced First Input Delay (FID) as a Core Web Vital. What is the key difference in what INP measures compared to FID?
options: A) INP measures only the first interaction on a page, exactly like FID did

B) INP measures the full latency of interactions across the entire page lifecycle (using a high percentile, effectively the worst typical interaction) — from input delay through event processing to the next paint — whereas FID only measured the delay before an event handler started running, and only for the very first interaction
C) INP is a lab-only synthetic metric that cannot be measured from real users in the field
D) INP measures scroll-jank, replacing FID's focus on click and tap responsiveness
questions.correctAnswer: B) INP measures the full latency of interactions across the entire page lifecycle (using a high percentile, effectively the worst typical interaction) — from input delay through event processing to the next paint — whereas FID only measured the delay before an event handler started running, and only for the very first interaction
questions.explanation: FID captured only 'input delay' (time before the handler starts) for the first interaction, missing slow handlers, re-render time, and paint time, and it ignored every interaction after the first. INP samples all (or nearly all) interactions during a page's lifetime and reports a high-percentile value, and it end-to-end measures input delay + processing time + presentation delay — a far more complete responsiveness signal.

questions.question: Per Google's Core Web Vitals thresholds, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads (segmented across mobile and desktop), which set of values classifies a page as 'Good' across all three metrics?
questions.explanation: The 'Good' thresholds are LCP ≤ 2.5s, CLS ≤ 0.1, and INP ≤ 200ms, all assessed at the 75th percentile of collected field data. Option B lists the 'Needs Improvement' upper bounds (anything above those is 'Poor'), not the 'Good' thresholds.

questions.question: Explain the difference between 'field data' (e.g., Chrome UX Report / RUM) and 'lab data' (e.g., Lighthouse, local DevTools) for Core Web Vitals, and why both matter to a frontend team.
questions.correctAnswer: Field data is Real User Monitoring collected from actual visitors' browsers (via the Chrome UX Report, or your own RUM/analytics pipeline using the web-vitals JS library), reflecting real network conditions, real devices, real content/personalization, and typically reported as a 75th-percentile value over a rolling ~28-day window. This is the data Google actually uses as a Search ranking signal. Lab data is synthetic and reproducible — generated by tools like Lighthouse or PageSpeed Insights' lab section under fixed, simulated network/CPU throttling profiles in a single run, with no real user interactions (so INP in particular can't be measured in a pure lab run — Lighthouse instead approximates responsiveness via Total Blocking Time). Lab data is valuable for fast, deterministic debugging and for catching regressions in CI/PR checks before shipping; field data is the ground truth for actual user experience and SEO/ranking impact, but is noisier, slower to accumulate, and can't be bisected to a single commit as easily. Mature teams use lab data as a guardrail and field data as the source of truth.
questions.explanation: Grading focus: correctly distinguishes RUM/CrUX (real users, ranking signal, percentile-based, no fixed conditions) from Lighthouse/lab (synthetic, reproducible, no real INP measurement, good for CI), and articulates why each is used for a different purpose (regression prevention vs. ground truth).

questions.question: List and briefly justify at least four concrete engineering techniques to improve LCP on a marketing landing page where the LCP element is a large hero image.
questions.correctAnswer: 1) Preload the hero image with <link rel="preload" as="image" href="..." fetchpriority="high"> so the browser's preload scanner discovers and starts fetching it as early as possible, instead of waiting for CSS/JS to reveal it. 2) Never lazy-load the LCP candidate — loading="lazy" defers fetch discovery until it's known to be near the viewport, directly delaying LCP; use fetchpriority="high" and omit loading="lazy" for above-the-fold hero images. 3) Serve a modern compressed format (WebP/AVIF) with a responsive srcset/sizes so mobile clients don't download an oversized desktop asset, reducing download time. 4) Reduce server response time / Time to First Byte (edge caching, CDN, SSR streaming, faster origin) since LCP is lower-bounded by TTFB — nothing can render before bytes arrive. 5) Eliminate render-blocking resources above the hero (defer non-critical CSS/JS, inline critical above-the-fold CSS) so the browser can start painting sooner. 6) Serve static assets from a CDN with HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 and long-lived cache-control headers to cut connection and round-trip latency.
questions.explanation: Looking for at least four distinct, correctly justified techniques spanning discovery/priority (preload, fetchpriority, avoiding lazy-load), payload (format/responsive images), and delivery/server (TTFB, render-blocking resources, CDN).

questions.question: Interaction to Next Paint (INP) decomposes a single interaction into three phases. Name the three phases and explain what you would specifically optimize in each to reduce INP.
questions.correctAnswer: 1) Input delay: the time from the user's physical input (click/tap/keypress) until the browser's main thread is free to begin running the associated event handlers. It's dominated by main-thread contention — long tasks from other JS execution, parsing/compiling scripts, or third-party code running at that moment. Optimize by breaking up long tasks (code-splitting, yielding via scheduler.yield()/setTimeout/requestIdleCallback), reducing total JS shipped/executed on load, and deferring non-critical third-party scripts so the thread is free when interactions happen. 2) Processing time: the time actually spent running the event handler(s) and any synchronous work they trigger (state updates, re-renders, synchronous DOM reads/writes). Optimize by minimizing handler complexity, deferring non-essential work (analytics, logging) off the critical path via requestIdleCallback/queueMicrotask/scheduler.postTask, using React's startTransition/useTransition to deprioritize expensive derived-state updates, avoiding layout thrashing by batching DOM reads and writes, and memoizing expensive computations. 3) Presentation delay: the time from the end of processing until the browser actually paints the next frame — style recalculation, layout, paint, and compositing, plus any wait for the next rendering opportunity (e.g., chained requestAnimationFrame calls). Optimize by minimizing the size/complexity of the DOM subtree being updated, avoiding forced synchronous reflow, preferring compositor-only properties (transform/opacity) over layout-triggering ones, and not needlessly chaining multiple rAF callbacks before the visual update lands.
questions.explanation: Grading focus: correctly names all three phases (input delay, processing time, presentation delay) and ties each to a specific, technically accurate optimization strategy rather than generic 'make it faster' advice.

questions.correctAnswer: Issue 1 — unsized image: `` has no `width`/`height` attributes (or CSS `aspect-ratio`), so the browser can't reserve its box before the image downloads; when it loads, it pushes the paragraph below it downward, causing a shift. Fix: add explicit `width`/`height` attributes (the browser derives an aspect ratio from them automatically) or set `aspect-ratio` in CSS so space is reserved from first paint. Issue 2 — content injected into an unsized container: `#promo-banner` starts empty with no reserved height, then an async fetch injects a `.banner` div into it later, shoving everything below it down the moment the response arrives. Fix: give `#promo-banner` a `min-height` matching the expected banner size (or render a skeleton placeholder of that size) so its box is stable before and after the content loads. Issue 3 — unoptimized web font swap: `@font-face` has no `font-display` strategy, so depending on the browser default this can cause FOIT/FOUT; if the fallback font's metrics (x-height, width) differ notably from 'Brand', the swap re-wraps text and shifts layout. Fix: preload the font file (``) and use `font-display: optional` (avoids the swap entirely if the font isn't ready in time) or use `size-adjust`/`ascent-override`/`descent-override` on a fallback `@font-face` to closely match the custom font's metrics so any swap causes minimal shift.
questions.explanation: Tests recognition of the three most common real-world CLS root causes: missing image dimensions, unreserved space for late-injected async content, and web font swap/FOIT-FOUT — plus the correct, specific fix for each.

Tests the ability to spot a compound LCP failure: an anti-pattern lazy-load on the LCP element itself, plus a client-fetch waterfall that hides the resource from the browser's early preload scanner, plus a missing priority hint — and to fix it by moving resolution server-side, preloading, and prioritizing.

Tests the ability to trace a laggy-typing INP regression to synchronous expensive work inside an event handler, and to apply React 18 concurrent-rendering primitives (useTransition/startTransition) correctly to separate urgent visual updates from deferrable computation, plus recognize analytics/off-critical-path deferral and worker/indexing as further mitigations.
